what_its_for: This insulin device delivers exactly 20 units of insulin under your skin (subcutaneously) to help control your blood sugar levels. Insulin is used to manage Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes by helping your body use sugar properly.
how_to_take: 1. Wash your hands well with soap and water. 2. Check the insulin — it should look clear (or evenly cloudy for some types). Do NOT use it if it looks discolored, has particles, or has changed appearance. 3. Choose an injection site: your belly (at least 2 inches from your belly button), outer thighs, upper arms, or buttocks. Rotate sites each time to avoid skin irritation. 4. Clean the skin with an alcohol wipe and let it dry completely. 5. Pinch the skin gently if needed. 6. Insert the needle at a 90-degree angle (or 45 degrees if you are very thin). 7. Press the button or plunger to deliver the full 20-unit dose. Hold in place for 10 seconds before removing. 8. Do NOT rub the injection site after. 9. Dispose of the used needle safely in a sharps container — never recap or reuse needles.
dosing: Your device is pre-set to deliver 20 units per dose. Use this device exactly as your doctor or diabetes care team instructed. Your dose timing depends on the type of insulin you are using — for example, rapid-acting insulin is usually taken just before or with meals, while long-acting insulin may be taken once or twice daily at set times. Do NOT change your dose or timing without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, what you should do depends on the type of insulin. For rapid-acting insulin (taken with meals): if you forgot before eating and your meal is done, skip that dose and resume at your next meal — do NOT double up. For long-acting insulin (once daily): take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose. Never take two doses at the same time. Call your doctor if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Unopened insulin: Store in the refrigerator (36°F to 46°F / 2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze insulin — throw it away if it has been frozen. In-use device: Once opened or in use, most insulin can be kept at room temperature (below 86°F / 30°C) for up to 28 days, depending on the brand — check your specific product instructions. Keep insulin away from direct sunlight and heat. Do NOT leave it in a hot car or near stoves or windows.
what_to_avoid: Avoid injecting into skin that is bruised, swollen, scarred, or hardened. Do not inject into the same spot repeatedly — always rotate your sites. Avoid drinking alcohol in large amounts, as it can cause your blood sugar to drop dangerously low. Avoid skipping meals after taking rapid-acting insulin. Do not stop taking insulin suddenly without your doctor's guidance, even if you feel well. Avoid vigorous exercise right after injecting insulin without eating, as this may lower your blood sugar too much.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you experience: signs of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) such as shakiness, sweating, confusion, fast heartbeat, dizziness, or fainting; signs of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) such as extreme thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, or fruity-smelling breath; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of your face or throat, or difficulty breathing; redness, swelling, or pain at your injection site that does not go away; or if your blood sugar readings are consistently too high or too low.
when_it_works: Rapid-acting insulin starts working within 15 minutes and peaks in about 1 to 2 hours. Long-acting insulin starts working within 1 to 2 hours and works steadily for up to 24 hours or more. You will not feel insulin working right away, but regular use as prescribed will help keep your blood sugar in a healthy range over time.
special_populations: Older adults: Blood sugar levels may be harder to predict and hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) can be more dangerous. Monitor closely and follow your doctor's dosing guidance. Children and teens: Insulin needs change with growth — regular check-ins with your care team are important. Pregnancy: Insulin is generally safe during pregnancy, but doses often need to be adjusted. Tell your doctor immediately if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Kidney or liver disease: These conditions can affect how long insulin stays active in your body, increasing the risk of low blood sugar. Extra monitoring may be needed.
